--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.degree_distribution()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get degree distribution as a mapping from degree to count. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.degree_distribution()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get degree distribution as a mapping from degree to count. title: >- [Graph.degree_distribution()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Get degree distribution as a mapping from degree to count. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get degree distribution as a mapping from degree to count. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L56577-L56678){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.degree_distribution() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Degree distribution](../assets/graphs/degree-distribution.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph with each node's degree in a badge, and a bar chart of how many nodes have each degree: one node of degree 1, one of degree 2, and three of degree 3." width="100%"} Returns a histogram of node degrees, showing how many nodes have each degree value. Useful for analyzing network topology and identifying hub nodes or scale-free properties. Each node is counted once, under its degree. Only degree values that occur appear as keys, so there are no zero-count entries, and the counts add up to the number of nodes. The distribution is a compact fingerprint of a network's structure: - a long tail of rare, very high degrees points to hubs and a possibly scale-free network - a narrow peak around one value suggests a regular or random-like network - a large count at degree `0` or `1` reveals many isolated or peripheral nodes In undirected graphs the degrees match `get_degree()` (parallel edges each count and a self-loop counts twice). In directed graphs, each node is binned by its total degree (in-degree plus out-degree), also matching `get_degree()`. Edge weights are ignored. The dictionary is not ordered by degree; wrap it in `sorted()` to read it in order. An empty graph gives an empty dictionary. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping degree values to the number of nodes with that degree. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~degrees`) : Each node's degree, rather than counts per degree. [](`~average_degree`) : The mean degree as a single number. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The distribution maps each degree to the number of nodes that have it. The four spokes of a star each have degree `1`, and the hub alone has degree `4`: ::: {#58b41853 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec star = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("Hub", "A"), ("Hub", "B"), ("Hub", "C"), ("Hub", "D")] ) star.degree_distribution() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: 4, 4: 1} ``` ::: ::: ### Hubs, or chance? In the Les Misérables network, characters are joined when they appear in the same chapter. A random graph with the same 77 nodes and 254 edges has the same average degree, about 6.6, so comparing the two distributions shows what the story adds to chance: ::: {#0786772f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl novel = ec.les_miserables() chance = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(77, 254, seed=2) counts = novel.degree_distribution(), chance.degree_distribution() pl.DataFrame( [ (degree, counts[0].get(degree, 0), counts[1].get(degree, 0)) for degree in sorted(counts[0].keys() | counts[1].keys()) ], schema=["degree", "novel", "random"], orient="row", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The random graph's degrees bunch around the average: no node has fewer than 2 edges or more than 13. The novel's spread both ways. 17 characters appear with only one other, and 7 main characters, with Valjean at 36, meet more people than anyone does in the random graph. The novel is on the left, with those 7 in the accent color and the 17 in the soft one, and the random graph is on the right: ::: {#01cfd427 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} degree = novel.degrees(return_dict=True) hubs = [character for character, d in degree.items() if d > 13] loners = [character for character, d in degree.items() if d == 1] ``` ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#2d22c852 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel.plot( highlight={"accent": hubs, "soft": loners}, show_labels=False, seed=1, width=360, height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
